title: Data Structures in Depth — Stacks, Queues, Trees & Hashing
subject: cs

questions.prompt: A stack is best described as:
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a stack is LIFO: the last item pushed is the first popped.
questions.feedbackWrong: Stacks are LIFO — push and pop happen at the same end, so the most recent item leaves first.

mistakes.correction: FIFO is a QUEUE — items leave at the opposite end they arrive. A stack only has one working end.

questions.prompt: Which application most naturally uses a circular queue?
options: Undo history in a text editor
Print jobs waiting for a printer with a fixed-size buffer
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — print buffers reuse fixed memory circularly; jobs are FIFO.
questions.feedbackWrong: Print job buffers are FIFO with fixed memory — a circular queue reuses freed slots. Undo, recursion and backtracking are all stack-shaped.

mistakes.correction: Undo must reverse the MOST RECENT action first — that's LIFO, a stack.

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between pre-order, in-order and post-order traversal of a binary tree, and state which one outputs a binary SEARCH tree's values in ascending order.

markScheme.text: Pre-order visits root, then left subtree, then right; post-order visits left, right, root last.
In-order visits left subtree, then root, then right subtree.
IN-ORDER traversal of a binary search tree yields ascending order — left subtree values are smaller, right larger.

mistakes.misconception: Believes root-first traversal produces sorted output.
mistakes.correction: The root is visited before either subtree in pre-order, so values appear in insertion-shaped order, not sorted order.

questions.prompt: Explain how a hash table stores key-value pairs, what a collision is, and one method of resolving collisions.

markScheme.text: A hash function maps the key to an index/address in the table where the value is stored.
Collision: two different keys hash to the SAME index.
Resolution by chaining — each slot holds a linked list of colliding entries.
Or open addressing — probe subsequent slots (linear/quadratic) until a free one is found. Either method credited.

questions.prompt: A 2D array A is stored with dimensions 10 rows × 8 columns of 4-byte values, starting at base address 1000, in row-major order. Calculate the byte address of element A[3][5] (zero-indexed).
Compared with an array, a linked list's main advantage is:
options: Efficient insertion and deletion without shifting elements
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — pointer rewiring inserts/removes in O(1) given the position, no shifting.
questions.feedbackWrong: Linked lists insert/delete by rewiring pointers — no element shifting. Arrays win on random access, memory density and cache use.

mistakes.misconception: Assumes all list-like structures support fast indexing.
mistakes.correction: Linked lists require traversal from the head — index access is O(n), arrays are O(1).

questions.prompt: Give two ways of representing a graph in memory and one advantage of each.

markScheme.text: Adjacency matrix — 2D array marking edges; advantage: O(1) edge lookup, simple for dense graphs.
Adjacency list — each vertex lists its neighbours; advantage: memory proportional to edges, efficient for sparse graphs.
Matrix wastes memory on sparse graphs while lists make edge-existence checks slower — a trade-off.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a static data structure (e.g. array) and a dynamic one (e.g. linked list) in terms of memory allocation.

markScheme.text: Static structures allocate a FIXED block of memory at creation/compile time.
Dynamic structures allocate memory node-by-node at runtime as elements are added, and free it on removal.
Consequence: arrays can't grow beyond their allocation but have no per-element overhead; linked structures grow freely but pay pointer memory and allocation cost.
